name: Environment & Agriculture
tagline: Explore living landscapes, grow understanding, and research resilient food systems.

nodes.title: Living Things Share Places
nodes.goal: Notice plants, animals, and nonliving parts of a place while observing gently.
learning_outcomes: Distinguish familiar living and nonliving parts of a place.
Describe one way a living thing uses its surroundings.
Observe without disturbing unfamiliar organisms.

lesson.overview: A place outdoors can include plants, animals, water, rocks, air, and soil. Living things use parts of that place in different ways: a bird may perch in a tree while an insect rests under a leaf. We can notice what is present without moving every object or taking every living thing home. Looking, listening, drawing, and asking an adult are ways to investigate. A careful observer describes what they see and leaves room for things they have not yet noticed.
lesson.worked_example: A child sees a tree, a stone, and a bird in a garden. The tree and bird are living things; the stone is nonliving. The bird uses a branch as a resting place, so the tree is also part of its surroundings.
lesson.activity: With an adult, observe a garden, park, or picture of a habitat. Point to two living and two nonliving things. Draw one connection without touching unfamiliar plants or animals.
lesson.reflection: What might live in the picture that you cannot see at first?

quiz.prompt: Which thing is living?
choices: A tree
A stone
A bench
quiz.answer: A tree
quiz.explain: A tree grows and is a living organism; a stone and bench are nonliving.
quiz.say: Which thing is living?

quiz.prompt: A bird sits on a branch. What is the branch giving it?
choices: A pair of shoes
A glass of milk
A place to rest
quiz.answer: A place to rest
quiz.explain: The branch supports the bird as a resting place.
quiz.say: A bird sits on a branch. What is the branch giving it?

quiz.prompt: How can you look at an unfamiliar insect gently?
choices: Put it in your pocket
Watch it without grabbing it
Squeeze it tightly
quiz.answer: Watch it without grabbing it
quiz.explain: Watching lets you learn while leaving the insect in its surroundings.
quiz.say: How can you look at an unfamiliar insect gently?

quiz.prompt: Which is a nonliving part of a pond picture?
choices: Water
A frog
A water plant
quiz.answer: Water
quiz.explain: Water supports life, but it is not itself a living organism.
quiz.say: Which is a nonliving part of a pond picture?

quiz.prompt: You cannot see any worms on the soil. Does that prove none are there?
choices: Yes, worms stay on the surface
Yes, hidden things do not exist
No
quiz.answer: No
quiz.explain: Some living things are small or hidden, so not seeing them is not proof of absence.
quiz.say: You cannot see any worms on the soil. Does that prove none are there?

quiz.prompt: Which statement tells what you actually noticed?
choices: No other animals exist
I saw one bird on the fence
This fence is the bird’s whole home
quiz.answer: I saw one bird on the fence
quiz.explain: A specific observation says what you saw without claiming more than you know.
quiz.say: Which statement tells what you actually noticed?

nodes.kid_text: Look closely at a place. You might see a plant, a bird, a rock, and water. Some things are living and some are not. Watch gently and leave living things in their homes.

nodes.title: Seeds and Growing Gardens
nodes.goal: Recognize a seed and observe how a cared-for plant changes over time.
learning_outcomes: Recognize seeds as part of plant life.
Put observed growth changes in time order.
Describe differences without expecting every seed to grow identically.

lesson.overview: A seed contains a young plant and stored resources that can support its first growth. Different seeds look different, and they do not all begin growing at the same speed. A growing plant changes over days: a root may appear before a shoot and leaves. A garden is a place people care for plants, but plants can also grow in many other places. Young learners can draw changes and ask an adult to help with planting, water, and safe handling.
lesson.worked_example: An adult plants a bean seed in a clear container for observation. On the first day the child sees only the seed. Later a root appears, followed by a shoot. A second seed grows later, showing that living things do not follow identical clocks.
lesson.activity: With adult help, observe a planted seed or a sequence of plant photographs for several days. Draw what you see each time, label the day, and keep seeds out of mouths.
lesson.reflection: What changed between your first and last drawing?

quiz.prompt: What can grow from a seed under suitable conditions?
choices: A plant
A metal spoon
A shoe
quiz.answer: A plant
quiz.explain: Seeds are part of the life cycle of seed plants.
quiz.say: What can grow from a seed under suitable conditions?

quiz.prompt: Which part usually grows down into the growing medium?
choices: A flower petal
A bird wing
A root
quiz.answer: A root
quiz.explain: Roots usually grow into the medium where they can take up water and help anchor the plant.
quiz.say: Which part usually grows down into the growing medium?

quiz.prompt: Why draw your plant on different days?
choices: To stop the plant from growing
To notice changes over time
To choose a pot color
quiz.answer: To notice changes over time
quiz.explain: A sequence of drawings records how the plant changes.
quiz.say: Why draw your plant on different days?

quiz.prompt: Two seeds begin growing on different days. Is that possible?
choices: Yes
No, seeds follow the same clock
No, roots appear at the same moment
quiz.answer: Yes
quiz.explain: Seeds can differ, and growing conditions may differ too.
quiz.say: Two seeds begin growing on different days. Is that possible?

quiz.prompt: Who should help you decide where to plant a seed?
choices: A toy bus
A television advertisement alone
A trusted adult
quiz.answer: A trusted adult
quiz.explain: An adult can help with suitable materials and safe handling.
quiz.say: Who should help you decide where to plant a seed?

quiz.prompt: Which drawing shows a change after a root appears?
choices: A later drawing of an empty chair
A later drawing with a shoot as well
An identical blank page
quiz.answer: A later drawing with a shoot as well
quiz.explain: A shoot is another stage of visible plant growth after the first observed root.
quiz.say: Which drawing shows a change after a root appears?

nodes.kid_text: A little seed can grow into a plant. Watch with a grown-up and draw what changes. Roots, shoots, and leaves may appear on different days.

nodes.title: Soil Is More Than Dirt
nodes.goal: Describe soil as a mixture and compare its visible properties using a fair observation.
learning_outcomes: Name living and nonliving components of soil.
Compare water movement while keeping test conditions similar.
Avoid claiming that one visible property measures all soil quality.

lesson.overview: Soil contains mineral particles, organic material, water, air spaces, and living organisms. It differs from place to place and from top to deeper layers. A dark color alone does not prove that one soil will grow every plant better. We can compare texture, visible plant pieces, and how water moves through equal samples while controlling the amount of water and container shape. Classroom observations reveal some properties, but they do not measure every nutrient or establish that a soil is safe to handle or grow food in.
lesson.worked_example: Two equal samples are placed in matching containers with drainage holes. The same measured water is added. One drains faster. This is evidence about water movement in these samples, not proof that it has more nutrients or is better for every plant.
lesson.activity: Use adult-provided clean potting materials in a tray. Compare appearance and a small equal-water drainage test, record observations, then wash hands. Do not collect from unknown or contaminated sites.
lesson.reflection: Why might a fast-draining material help one plant and be unsuitable for another?

quiz.prompt: Which list includes things that may be found in soil?
choices: Grains, air, water, and plant remains
One solid piece of rock
A container of pure water
quiz.answer: Grains, air, water, and plant remains
quiz.explain: Soil is a mixture with solids, spaces, water, and often living organisms.
quiz.say: Which list includes things that may be found in soil?

quiz.prompt: What should be equal in a fair drainage comparison?
choices: The result you wish to get
The names of the observers
The amount of water added
quiz.answer: The amount of water added
quiz.explain: Equal water input helps make differences in drainage interpretable.
quiz.say: What should be equal in a fair drainage comparison?

quiz.prompt: Dark soil must be best for every plant. Is that a sound conclusion?
choices: Yes, color measures the nutrients
No
Yes, color measures everything
quiz.answer: No
quiz.explain: Color is one observation and does not determine all plant needs or soil properties.
quiz.say: Dark soil must be best for every plant. Is that a sound conclusion?

quiz.prompt: What can small spaces between particles contain?
choices: Air or water
Pieces of polished metal
Nothing under any conditions
quiz.answer: Air or water
quiz.explain: Pore spaces can hold air and water in varying amounts.
quiz.say: What can small spaces between particles contain?

quiz.prompt: Why use clean materials supplied by an adult?
choices: Soil from different places is identical
Clean materials contain no particles
Unknown soil may contain unsafe things
quiz.answer: Unknown soil may contain unsafe things
quiz.explain: The source matters for safe handling; appearance alone cannot establish what soil contains.
quiz.say: Why use clean materials supplied by an adult?

quiz.prompt: A sample drains quickly. What did the test directly show?
choices: It is the best material for a cactus
Water moved through that sample quickly
It has a high nitrogen content
quiz.answer: Water moved through that sample quickly
quiz.explain: The observation concerns water movement under the test conditions.
quiz.say: A sample drains quickly. What did the test directly show?

nodes.kid_text: Soil is a mixture. It can hold tiny rock pieces, old plant parts, water, air, and living things. Compare two safe samples with a grown-up and describe what you really see.

nodes.title: From Farm to Plate and Back
nodes.goal: Trace a familiar food through growing, transport, preparation, and resource recovery.
learning_outcomes: Sequence several steps in a food system.
Identify people and resources behind a food item.
Distinguish preventing waste from handling scraps after they exist.

lesson.overview: Food reaches people through connected steps. Someone grows or raises it, others may harvest, store, transport, sell, prepare, and share it. These steps use land, water, energy, knowledge, and work. Some foods travel far and some nearby, but distance alone does not tell the whole environmental story. Avoiding unnecessary waste uses the resources already invested more carefully. Some plant scraps can enter a suitable managed compost system, where decomposers break them down; local guidance determines what a particular system accepts.
lesson.worked_example: A carrot grows in a field, travels to a shop, and becomes part of a meal. A peeled scrap may enter a suitable compost bin, while an uneaten whole carrot represents food and the resources used to grow and move it. Preventing avoidable waste comes before deciding how to dispose of it.
lesson.activity: Draw the journey of a fictional apple from tree to meal. Add the people and resources needed at three steps. With an adult, check a local compost system’s accepted-material list before sorting pretend scraps.
lesson.reflection: Which parts of a food’s journey are easy to overlook when you see it in a shop?

quiz.prompt: What happens before a carrot is harvested?
choices: It grows
It is eaten in a meal
It becomes a shopping bag
quiz.answer: It grows
quiz.explain: Harvesting gathers food after it has grown.
quiz.say: What happens before a carrot is harvested?

quiz.prompt: Which person is part of a food’s journey?
choices: A person repairing an unrelated roof
No one until it reaches a plate
A worker who transports it
quiz.answer: A worker who transports it
quiz.explain: Food systems include many people across growing, transport, sale, and preparation.
quiz.say: Which person is part of a food’s journey?

quiz.prompt: Which resource may be used while food is grown?
choices: Water
A shop barcode label
A finished shopping receipt
quiz.answer: Water
quiz.explain: Water is one of the resources used in producing food.
quiz.say: Which resource may be used while food is grown?

quiz.prompt: What is a helpful way to reduce avoidable food waste?
choices: Plan to use the food already available
Discard usable food without checking
Buy more without checking
quiz.answer: Plan to use the food already available
quiz.explain: Using available food can prevent waste before disposal becomes necessary.
quiz.say: What is a helpful way to reduce avoidable food waste?

quiz.prompt: Can every compost bin accept exactly the same scraps?
choices: Yes, bins accept the same materials
Yes, matching colors mean matching rules
No, check that system’s guidance
quiz.answer: No, check that system’s guidance
quiz.explain: Composting systems differ in materials, operation, and accepted inputs.
quiz.say: Can every compost bin accept exactly the same scraps?

quiz.prompt: Does a short travel distance alone prove a food has the smallest environmental impact?
choices: Yes, growing uses no resources
No
Yes, nothing else matters
quiz.answer: No
quiz.explain: Growing, storage, transport method, and other stages also influence impact.
quiz.say: Does a short travel distance alone prove a food has the smallest environmental impact?

nodes.title: Farms as Living Systems
nodes.goal: Explain how crops, soil organisms, pollinators, and predators interact in an agroecosystem.
learning_outcomes: Represent multiple ecological interactions on a farm.
Distinguish an ecosystem function from a guaranteed production outcome.
Predict direct and indirect consequences of a change.

lesson.overview: A farm is both a production system and an ecosystem. Crops interact with soil organisms, competing plants, herbivores, predators, pollinators, and people. Biodiversity can support functions such as decomposition and pollination, but effects depend on which organisms are present and on local conditions. A food web shows feeding relationships; other networks show pollination or nutrient movement. Managing one part can affect another, so a useful model makes these connections explicit without assuming that every species always helps every farming goal.
lesson.worked_example: A flowering border provides habitat for several insects. Some visit crop flowers; others eat crop-feeding insects. If observations show more visitors, that alone does not prove a higher harvest. A harvest comparison and information about weather and field differences are also needed.
lesson.activity: Draw a farm network containing a crop, decomposers, a herbivore, a predator, and a pollinator. Label each arrow with its meaning and predict two possible effects of removing one organism.
lesson.reflection: Which connections in your diagram are supported by observations, and which are hypotheses?

quiz.prompt: What is an agroecosystem?
choices: Farming with its ecological interactions
Machinery used for producing a harvest
A crop’s genetic classification system
quiz.answer: Farming with its ecological interactions
quiz.explain: The term includes production, organisms, environmental conditions, and their interactions.

quiz.prompt: Which organisms help break down dead organic material?
choices: Pollinators
Herbivores
Decomposers
quiz.answer: Decomposers
quiz.explain: Decomposers process organic material and contribute to nutrient cycling.

quiz.prompt: A pollinator-visitation count rises. What does it directly measure?
choices: Total reproduction of the crop plants
Observed visits during the sample period
Annual mass of the harvested crop
quiz.answer: Observed visits during the sample period
quiz.explain: Visitor counts describe visitation, while crop output requires its own measurement.

quiz.prompt: A predator eats a crop-feeding insect. What interaction links them?
choices: Predation
Pollination
Competition
quiz.answer: Predation
quiz.explain: One organism consuming another is predation.

quiz.prompt: Why label arrows in a farm diagram?
choices: Arrow thickness can replace process descriptions
The same arrow automatically means feeding
Different arrows can represent different processes
quiz.answer: Different arrows can represent different processes
quiz.explain: Different processes connect organisms, so labels make the model interpretable.

quiz.prompt: Removing a herbivore may affect a predator. What kind of link is this?
choices: A change in the predator’s classification
A dependency within the food web
A nutrient input from the atmosphere
quiz.answer: A dependency within the food web
quiz.explain: Predators may depend on herbivores as prey, creating a linked response.

quiz.prompt: Does adding any species always improve a farm?
choices: No; species effects depend on context
Yes; added diversity guarantees higher harvests
Yes; species number determines crop value
quiz.answer: No; species effects depend on context
quiz.explain: Species can support, compete with, or damage different functions depending on context.

quiz.prompt: Which comparison better tests a border planting’s effect on yield?
choices: A single photograph before and after border planting
A preference survey about flowering-border appearance
Replicated comparable plots with and without borders
quiz.answer: Replicated comparable plots with and without borders
quiz.explain: A relevant comparison and replicated outcomes help separate an effect from other differences.

quiz.prompt: What is an ecosystem service in this context?
choices: An accounting fee for measuring field boundaries
An ecosystem contribution benefiting people
A machine service provided to farm operators
quiz.answer: An ecosystem contribution benefiting people
quiz.explain: Examples include pollination, nutrient cycling contributions, and water regulation relevant to people.

quiz.prompt: Why include humans in a farm-system diagram?
choices: Management changes resources and interactions
Human presence fixes the ecosystem’s productivity
Management decisions remove ecological dependence
quiz.answer: Management changes resources and interactions
quiz.explain: Planting, harvesting, irrigation, and land-use choices shape the system.

quiz.prompt: After planting a flowering border, observers count more insects. Explain why this alone does not establish improved crop yield and propose a stronger test.
quiz.answer: Insect visits measure one interaction, not harvest yield. Compare yield in comparable plots with and without the border, use replication, and record weather or other differences. The comparison helps test whether ecological changes correspond to the claimed production outcome.
quiz.explain: Insect visits measure one interaction, not harvest yield. Compare yield in comparable plots with and without the border, use replication, and record weather or other differences. The comparison helps test whether ecological changes correspond to the claimed production outcome.

nodes.title: Water Budgets in Gardens and Farms
nodes.goal: Account for water inputs, outputs, and storage and compare strategies within a clear boundary.
learning_outcomes: Calculate storage change from a simple water balance.
Distinguish infiltration from water leaving a chosen system.
Explain why water-saving claims depend on boundaries and measurements.

lesson.overview: A water budget follows water through a defined place and period. Rainfall and irrigation can enter; runoff, drainage, evaporation, and plant transpiration can leave; some water remains stored in soil. The change in storage equals inputs minus outputs when all relevant flows are included. A diagram helps prevent double counting: water infiltrating the surface is not automatically a loss from the whole soil system. Water-saving claims need a boundary, because reducing withdrawals at one farm may also change return flows used elsewhere.
lesson.worked_example: A hypothetical garden receives 30 litres of rain and 20 litres of irrigation during a period. Runoff is 5 litres, drainage 10, and evaporation plus transpiration 25. Inputs total 50 and outputs total 40, so stored water increases by 10 litres under this simplified budget.
lesson.activity: Make a water-flow diagram using the example. Change one input and calculate the storage change. Then list flows or measurements that a real investigation would need to include.
lesson.reflection: When might a method that reduces visible runoff fail to reduce total water consumption?

quiz.prompt: Inputs are 50 litres and outputs are 40 litres. What is storage change?
choices: Storage increases by 10 litres
Storage decreases by 10 litres
Storage increases by 90 litres
quiz.answer: Storage increases by 10 litres
quiz.explain: Storage change equals inputs minus outputs: 50 - 40 = 10 litres.

quiz.prompt: What is transpiration?
choices: Liquid-water entry into soil
Surface-water flow across land
Water-vapor loss from plants
quiz.answer: Water-vapor loss from plants
quiz.explain: Plants release water vapor, largely through leaf openings.

quiz.prompt: Water enters the soil surface. What is that process called?
choices: Condensation
Infiltration
Evaporation
quiz.answer: Infiltration
quiz.explain: Infiltration is water entering the soil at its surface.

quiz.prompt: Is infiltration necessarily an output from a boundary that includes the soil?
choices: No; it may remain inside the boundary
Yes; entry into soil is external discharge
Yes; infiltration is counted as evaporation
quiz.answer: No; it may remain inside the boundary
quiz.explain: Within a soil-inclusive boundary, infiltration can be an internal transfer or an input rather than a loss.

quiz.prompt: Which information is needed for a water budget?
choices: The average color of the growing crop
The typeface used to label the water tank
A defined boundary and time interval
quiz.answer: A defined boundary and time interval
quiz.explain: Accounting depends on which place and interval the flows refer to.

quiz.prompt: If outputs exceed inputs, what can happen to stored water?
choices: Storage remains fixed
Storage can decrease
Storage must increase
quiz.answer: Storage can decrease
quiz.explain: A negative input-minus-output balance draws down stored water if the accounting is complete.

quiz.prompt: What is runoff?
choices: Surface flow across the land
Water vapor released by leaves
Water held within soil pores
quiz.answer: Surface flow across the land
quiz.explain: Runoff moves along the surface and may leave the selected area.

quiz.prompt: A watering method uses less withdrawn water but reduces downstream return flow. What should be checked?
choices: The irrigator’s equipment purchase price
The visible diameter of the supply pipe
The wider catchment water balance
quiz.answer: The wider catchment water balance
quiz.explain: Water available to others can change, so local withdrawal savings do not automatically equal basin savings.

quiz.prompt: Why combine evaporation and transpiration in some budgets?
choices: They describe water retained within the soil
They are often estimated as evapotranspiration
They are two names for root water uptake
quiz.answer: They are often estimated as evapotranspiration
quiz.explain: Evapotranspiration groups two water-vapor transfer processes when a combined estimate is useful.

quiz.prompt: A budget does not balance. What is a reasonable first investigation?
choices: Check missing flows and measurement errors
Infer the production of additional water
Discard the observation with the largest value
quiz.answer: Check missing flows and measurement errors
quiz.explain: Incomplete accounting and uncertain measurements can explain a residual.

quiz.prompt: A hypothetical plot receives 45 litres of rain and 15 litres of irrigation. Runoff is 8 litres, drainage 12, and evapotranspiration 30. Calculate storage change and state the accounting assumption.
quiz.answer: Inputs total 60 litres and outputs total 50 litres, so storage increases by 10 litres. The balance assumes the boundary and time period are fixed and relevant flows are included; omitted flows or measurement error would alter the estimate.
quiz.explain: Inputs total 60 litres and outputs total 50 litres, so storage increases by 10 litres. The balance assumes the boundary and time period are fixed and relevant flows are included; omitted flows or measurement error would alter the estimate.

visual_spec.title: A simplified garden water balance

items.label: 50 litres
items.detail: 30 rain plus 20 irrigation.

items.heading: Outputs
items.label: 40 litres

visual_spec.takeaway: A balance works only when the boundary and relevant flows are clear.

nodes.title: Soil, Nutrients, and Erosion
nodes.goal: Connect soil structure, nutrient cycles, and erosion while evaluating management tradeoffs.
learning_outcomes: Represent nutrient stocks and transfers without creating matter.
Distinguish erosion, leaching, and gaseous loss pathways.
Evaluate context-dependent management tradeoffs.

lesson.overview: Soil supports plants through its physical structure, water and air balance, chemical properties, and living communities. Nutrients move among mineral forms, organisms, organic matter, water, and the atmosphere; they are not created when a field is fertilized. Harvest exports some nutrients, and additions can replenish stocks, but excess or poorly timed inputs can leave the field through runoff, leaching, or gaseous losses. Erosion removes soil particles, often redistributing organic matter and nutrients with them. Management choices depend on soil, climate, crop, slope, and local constraints rather than a single universal recipe.
lesson.worked_example: A fictional field receives 80 units of a nutrient, exports 50 in harvest, loses an estimated 20 to other pathways, and stores 10 more than before. The balance closes, but the numerical surplus alone does not identify which management change would work: the loss pathway and timing matter.
lesson.activity: Construct a nutrient stock-and-flow diagram with stated hypothetical values. Compare bare soil and covered soil in published or supplied erosion observations, identify confounders, and explain why a classroom model is not a field recommendation.
lesson.reflection: How could a practice improve one soil function while creating a different challenge?

quiz.prompt: A field receives 80 nutrient units, exports 50, and loses 20. What is net storage change?
choices: +10 units
+150 units
−10 units
quiz.answer: +10 units
quiz.explain: Inputs minus outputs give 80 - 50 - 20 = 10 units retained in the simplified balance.

quiz.prompt: What does erosion directly move?
choices: Water vapor
Dissolved gases
Soil particles
quiz.answer: Soil particles
quiz.explain: Wind or water can detach and transport soil particles and associated material.

quiz.prompt: How does leaching differ from erosion?
choices: Organic carbon transfers from leaves to the air
Dissolved material travels through soil with water
Solid particles move across exposed soil surfaces
quiz.answer: Dissolved material travels through soil with water
quiz.explain: Leaching concerns dissolved material in percolating water; erosion involves particle transport.

quiz.prompt: Harvested crops can remove nutrients from a field. What follows?
choices: Include harvested nutrients as an output
Treat harvest as an internal nutrient source
Leave removed crop biomass outside the budget
quiz.answer: Include harvested nutrients as an output
quiz.explain: Nutrients incorporated in removed biomass are an output from the field boundary.

quiz.prompt: Why can soil cover reduce some erosion?
choices: It increases the force of incoming raindrops
It prevents dissolved nutrients from forming
It can shield soil and slow surface flow
quiz.answer: It can shield soil and slow surface flow
quiz.explain: Cover can protect the surface, though effectiveness depends on conditions and design.

quiz.prompt: Why is more nutrient input not always better?
choices: Inputs replace the need for water and sunlight
Inputs can exceed uptake and increase losses
Inputs are proportional to harvest without limits
quiz.answer: Inputs can exceed uptake and increase losses
quiz.explain: Nutrient uptake has limits; excess can be stored or lost rather than increasing useful production.

quiz.prompt: Which feature concerns soil’s physical structure?
choices: The arrangement of particles and pores
The concentration of dissolved mineral ions
The metabolic activity of soil organisms
quiz.answer: The arrangement of particles and pores
quiz.explain: Structure describes how particles and pores are organized, affecting water, air, and roots.

quiz.prompt: Two fields differ in cover and slope. What complicates attributing erosion differences to cover?
choices: Cover becomes unobservable on a sloping field
The smaller field becomes the control by definition
Slope may confound the cover comparison
quiz.answer: Slope may confound the cover comparison
quiz.explain: Different slope can affect erosion independently of cover.

quiz.prompt: Why specify nutrient units in a budget?
choices: Nutrient names are sufficient for a mass balance
Quantities must use compatible units and substances
Unit labels determine the direction of nutrient flows
quiz.answer: Quantities must use compatible units and substances
quiz.explain: A valid mass balance needs comparable quantities and a clear substance definition.

quiz.prompt: A model ignores gaseous nitrogen losses. What may result?
choices: An unexplained residual or overstated retention
A verified absence of gaseous transfer pathways
An automatic increase in measured crop removal
quiz.answer: An unexplained residual or overstated retention
quiz.explain: Omitting an actual output can make apparent storage larger than true storage.

quiz.prompt: A nutrient budget records 100 units added, 60 harvested, and 15 leached but ignores gaseous losses. Explain the apparent storage change and why it may be too high.
quiz.answer: The recorded balance gives 25 units of apparent storage. If gaseous losses occur, they are another output, so true retention is lower. A complete nutrient balance needs those losses or an explicit residual and uncertainty.
quiz.explain: The recorded balance gives 25 units of apparent storage. If gaseous losses occur, they are another output, so true retention is lower. A complete nutrient balance needs those losses or an explicit residual and uncertainty.

nodes.title: Food Systems, Land, and Resource Tradeoffs
nodes.goal: Compare food-system scenarios using multiple indicators, explicit functional units, and distributional effects.
learning_outcomes: Calculate and interpret resource indicators with functional units.
Distinguish food availability from access.
Evaluate tradeoffs and distribution rather than relying on one metric.

lesson.overview: Food systems aim to supply food while supporting livelihoods and managing land, water, energy, and biodiversity. An impact per kilogram, per serving, per unit of nutrition, and per hectare answers different questions. Higher yield can lower land used per unit of output while increasing some local pressures; outcomes also depend on what happens to any land no longer needed. Food availability is not the same as access: people may face price, transport, storage, or social barriers. Good comparisons report several indicators and uncertainties rather than collapsing all value judgments into a single ranking.
lesson.worked_example: Scenario A produces 4 tonnes on 2 hectares; B produces 6 tonnes on 2 hectares. Their yields are 2 and 3 tonnes per hectare. This tells us about land productivity, not water demand, labor conditions, nutrition, or whether lower-income households can obtain the food.
lesson.activity: Compare two fictional supply scenarios using land area, output, water withdrawal, energy, labor conditions, and access. Calculate two per-unit indicators and write a recommendation conditional on clearly stated priorities.
lesson.reflection: Which people or environmental effects disappear if you compare only cost per kilogram?

quiz.prompt: A farm produces 6 tonnes on 2 hectares. What is yield?
choices: 3 tonnes per hectare
12 tonnes per hectare
0.33 tonnes per hectare
quiz.answer: 3 tonnes per hectare
quiz.explain: Yield divides output by cultivated area: 6/2 = 3.

quiz.prompt: Why can per-kilogram and per-serving comparisons differ?
choices: A serving and a kilogram have identical meanings
The underlying measurements change with division
The comparison’s unit and function differ
quiz.answer: The comparison’s unit and function differ
quiz.explain: The functional unit determines what service or quantity is being compared.

quiz.prompt: A region has enough food in total but some households cannot afford it. What issue remains?
choices: Crop diversity
Food access
Food availability
quiz.answer: Food access
quiz.explain: Availability does not ensure that people can economically or physically obtain food.

quiz.prompt: Higher yield alone proves which conclusion?
choices: Greater measured output per cultivated area
Lower water use per unit of nutrition delivered
Better working conditions for harvesting workers
quiz.answer: Greater measured output per cultivated area
quiz.explain: Yield is an output-to-area ratio, not a complete sustainability assessment.

quiz.prompt: What is a functional unit?
choices: The particular equipment used for measurement
The total number of modeled environmental effects
The defined comparison quantity or service
quiz.answer: The defined comparison quantity or service
quiz.explain: A common functional unit makes alternative systems comparable for a stated purpose.

quiz.prompt: Why examine what happens to land supposedly spared by higher yields?
choices: Land area is unrelated to wider resource impacts
Land may shift to another productive use
Spared land is restored without further decisions
quiz.answer: Land may shift to another productive use
quiz.explain: Land-use outcomes depend on economic and policy responses, not yield alone.

quiz.prompt: Which indicator directly addresses a social concern?
choices: Working conditions
Irrigation volume
Fertilizer mass
quiz.answer: Working conditions
quiz.explain: Labor conditions concern the people whose work supports the food system.

quiz.prompt: A scenario improves one metric and worsens another. What should a comparison do?
choices: Select the improved metric as the sole objective
Treat the adverse metric as measurement error
Expose the tradeoff and decision priorities
quiz.answer: Expose the tradeoff and decision priorities
quiz.explain: Transparent tradeoffs allow a conditional and accountable choice.

quiz.prompt: Why report uncertainty ranges for resource estimates?
choices: Precise-looking estimates exclude model error
Input uncertainty can affect the comparison
Ranges make distinct scenarios equivalent
quiz.answer: Input uncertainty can affect the comparison
quiz.explain: Uncertainty makes the strength and stability of the comparison visible.

quiz.prompt: Which statement is justified if only transport distance is known?
choices: Distance describes one supply-chain feature
Distance establishes the complete lifecycle impact
Distance determines production-energy requirements
quiz.answer: Distance describes one supply-chain feature
quiz.explain: Transport mode, production, storage, and other stages require additional information.

quiz.prompt: Scenario A yields 8 tonnes on 4 hectares; B yields 9 tonnes on 3 hectares. Compare land productivity and explain two issues the ratio cannot decide.
quiz.answer: A yields 2 tonnes per hectare and B yields 3 tonnes per hectare. B has higher land productivity, but the ratio does not establish water demand, labor conditions, or food access. Those require separate indicators and a clear comparison boundary.
quiz.explain: A yields 2 tonnes per hectare and B yields 3 tonnes per hectare. B has higher land productivity, but the ratio does not establish water demand, labor conditions, or food access. Those require separate indicators and a clear comparison boundary.

nodes.title: Agroecological Systems and Resilience
nodes.goal: Analyze coupled ecological and management processes using feedbacks, diversity, thresholds, and resilience concepts.
learning_outcomes: Distinguish resistance, recovery, and resilience for specified functions.
Analyze diversity benefits under correlated disturbances.
Critique feedback and threshold claims in coupled systems.

lesson.overview: Agroecology examines ecological processes in agricultural systems together with management and social context. Diversity can provide response options when disturbances affect organisms differently, but its benefit depends on functional traits, interactions, and feasible management. Resilience concerns the capacity to absorb disturbance and reorganize while retaining specified functions; resistance and recovery are related but distinct. Feedbacks may stabilize a system or reinforce degradation, and thresholds may lead to qualitatively different states. A systems analysis specifies whose functions matter, at what scale, and over what time horizon rather than using resilience as a synonym for goodness.
lesson.worked_example: A diversified farm portfolio includes crops with different sensitivity to a modeled dry period. Its aggregate output falls less than that of a single crop in one scenario, but added labor and market constraints may offset benefits. Correlated failures under an extreme regional drought can also reduce the expected diversification advantage.
lesson.activity: Construct a causal-loop diagram of a hypothetical farming landscape. Identify a stabilizing loop, a reinforcing loop, a disturbance, and two valued functions. Use scenario analysis to compare resistance and recovery while stating social and ecological tradeoffs.
lesson.reflection: Resilience of what, to which disturbance, for whose benefit, and over what timescale?

quiz.prompt: A system changes little during a disturbance. Which property is most directly described?
choices: Resistance
Recovery rate
Response diversity
quiz.answer: Resistance
quiz.explain: Resistance describes how strongly the system initially responds to disturbance.

quiz.prompt: A system returns quickly after disturbance. Which property is most directly described?
choices: Resistance magnitude
Baseline productivity
Recovery rate
quiz.answer: Recovery rate
quiz.explain: Recovery rate concerns how rapidly a function returns following a change.

quiz.prompt: Why might crop diversity buffer aggregate output?
choices: Species number determines harvest stability
Different crops can respond differently
Crop failures are independent by definition
quiz.answer: Different crops can respond differently
quiz.explain: Different responses can reduce synchronized losses, but dependence and constraints matter.

quiz.prompt: What weakens diversification benefits?
choices: Correlated crop failures
Different response traits
Independent sales options
quiz.answer: Correlated crop failures
quiz.explain: If all components fail together, diversity provides less buffering.

quiz.prompt: Which is a reinforcing feedback?
choices: A sensor detects error and activates a correction
A reservoir fills and triggers reduced inflow
Soil loss reduces cover and increases further loss
quiz.answer: Soil loss reduces cover and increases further loss
quiz.explain: The initial change promotes more change in the same direction.

quiz.prompt: Why define the valued system function?
choices: A single output metric captures stakeholder values
A system may retain one function and lose another
The same resilience score applies to each function
quiz.answer: A system may retain one function and lose another
quiz.explain: The meaning of resilience depends on what persistence or performance is being assessed.

quiz.prompt: A threshold claim requires what kind of evidence?
choices: Evidence of a qualitative state change and alternatives
A fitted straight line through a short time series
A diagram identifying the preferred stable condition
quiz.answer: Evidence of a qualitative state change and alternatives
quiz.explain: Thresholds involve more than ordinary variation and should be supported by appropriate observations or models.

quiz.prompt: Why include labor and market conditions in an agroecological comparison?
choices: They determine ecological outcomes without biophysical data
They can be held constant across contexts without evidence
They influence feasibility and distribution of benefits
quiz.answer: They influence feasibility and distribution of benefits
quiz.explain: Ecological performance interacts with social and economic feasibility.

quiz.prompt: Can a harmful system be resilient?
choices: No; persistent states are classified as resistance
Yes; an undesirable state can be persistent
No; resilience implies a socially desirable state
quiz.answer: Yes; an undesirable state can be persistent
quiz.explain: Persistence is not itself an ethical judgment; the desirability of a state must be assessed separately.

quiz.prompt: What does a causal-loop diagram provide by itself?
choices: An organized hypothesis about feedbacks
An independently validated quantitative forecast
An identified causal effect for each drawn link
quiz.answer: An organized hypothesis about feedbacks
quiz.explain: The diagram organizes assumptions that still require evidence and testing.

quiz.prompt: A diversified farm withstands one dry season better but all crops fail under an extreme regional drought. Explain this using response diversity and dependence, then critique a claim of universal resilience.
quiz.answer: Response diversity can buffer output when crops react differently, but correlated failures reduce that benefit. Resilience must specify the disturbance, valued function, scale, and social constraints. One successful season cannot establish universal resilience across more severe events.
quiz.explain: Response diversity can buffer output when crops react differently, but correlated failures reduce that benefit. Resilience must specify the disturbance, valued function, scale, and social constraints. One successful season cannot establish universal resilience across more severe events.

nodes.title: Field Experiments and Spatial Evidence
nodes.goal: Design replicated field comparisons and analyze spatial heterogeneity without confusing subsamples with independent units.
learning_outcomes: Identify treatment units, subsamples, and independent replication.
Use blocking and randomization to address field heterogeneity.
Critique spatial dependence and remote-sensing validation.

lesson.overview: Field research must separate treatment effects from gradients in soil, slope, weather, and management history. Randomization reduces systematic treatment allocation bias; blocking groups relatively similar experimental units to improve precision. The unit assigned to a treatment determines independent replication: many soil cores from one treated field do not create many independently treated fields. Spatial and temporal dependence affect uncertainty, while measurement protocols and missing observations affect comparability. Remote sensing can broaden coverage, but spectral measurements need suitable ground information and cannot reveal every ecological or social variable.
lesson.worked_example: Four blocks each contain one randomly assigned treatment plot and one comparison plot. Five soil cores within each plot improve characterization of that plot, but treatment replication is four plots per condition, not twenty independent cores. Analysis should preserve the design and account for block differences.
lesson.activity: Write a field-study protocol for a fictional soil-cover comparison. Define plots, blocks, randomization, replication, subsampling, measurement dates, missing-data handling, and a spatial map. Critique the inference possible from one treated field and one untreated field.
lesson.reflection: When does collecting more measurements improve precision without increasing independent replication?

quiz.prompt: One field receives a treatment and yields 30 soil cores. How many independently treated fields are there?
choices: One independently treated field
Thirty independently treated fields
Thirty-one independently treated fields
quiz.answer: One independently treated field
quiz.explain: The field is the treatment unit; cores are subsamples within that unit.

quiz.prompt: What is the purpose of blocking?
choices: Assign the most promising treatment to the best soil
Replace independent replication with extra subsamples
Group comparable units before treatment comparisons
quiz.answer: Group comparable units before treatment comparisons
quiz.explain: Blocking can account for known gradients or nuisance variation and improve precision.

quiz.prompt: Why randomize treatment within blocks?
choices: Ensure the treatment effect is identical within blocks
Reduce systematic allocation differences within blocks
Make environmental conditions identical within blocks
quiz.answer: Reduce systematic allocation differences within blocks
quiz.explain: Randomization protects against deliberate or accidental treatment placement bias.

quiz.prompt: Nearby soil observations are strongly correlated. What does ignoring this risk?
choices: Overstating information and understating uncertainty
Understating information and overstating uncertainty
Increasing the number of independently assigned plots
quiz.answer: Overstating information and understating uncertainty
quiz.explain: Correlated samples carry less independent information than an equal number of independent observations.

quiz.prompt: What is pseudoreplication?
choices: Taking several measurements from different field units
Grouping similar plots before random assignment
Counting dependent subsamples as treatment replicates
quiz.answer: Counting dependent subsamples as treatment replicates
quiz.explain: The mistake inflates replication and can produce misleading uncertainty and significance.

quiz.prompt: Why collect ground measurements for a remote-sensing model?
choices: Establish universal transfer across unobserved climates
Link spectral measurements to the target quantity
Remove pixel-size differences between satellite sensors
quiz.answer: Link spectral measurements to the target quantity
quiz.explain: Ground information links remote measurements to the quantity of interest and tests accuracy.

quiz.prompt: Treatment and comparison plots are measured in different seasons. What is a concern?
choices: Season may be confounded with treatment
Seasonal change provides randomized replication
Season can be inferred from treatment assignment
quiz.answer: Season may be confounded with treatment
quiz.explain: Seasonal differences can explain outcomes independently of the treatment.

quiz.prompt: Which sampling record most supports reproducibility?
choices: Titles, photographs, affiliations, and preferred results
Outcomes, chart colors, report length, and author names
Locations, dates, methods, units, and inclusion rules
quiz.answer: Locations, dates, methods, units, and inclusion rules
quiz.explain: A traceable protocol lets others interpret and repeat the measurements.

quiz.prompt: A satellite model works in one region. What is needed before broad transfer?
choices: A relabeling of the original calibration observations
Validation under the new regional conditions
A larger geographic extent in the display settings
quiz.answer: Validation under the new regional conditions
quiz.explain: Different soils, crops, climates, and sensors can change the relationship between signal and target.

quiz.prompt: Why retain block identifiers in the dataset?
choices: They preserve the design structure for analysis
They independently establish a causal mechanism
They replace the need to retain outcome measurements
quiz.answer: They preserve the design structure for analysis
quiz.explain: The analysis should respect the grouping used to control variation in the design.

quiz.prompt: A researcher treats one field, samples 40 cores, and compares them with 40 cores from one untreated field. Explain the replication problem and improve the design.
quiz.answer: The field is the treatment unit, so cores are subsamples rather than independent treatment replication. Treating them as independent is pseudoreplication. Use multiple independently assigned fields or plots, with randomization and blocking where appropriate, and model within-unit dependence.
quiz.explain: The field is the treatment unit, so cores are subsamples rather than independent treatment replication. Treating them as independent is pseudoreplication. Use multiple independently assigned fields or plots, with randomization and blocking where appropriate, and model within-unit dependence.

nodes.title: Sustainability Transitions and Scenario Analysis
nodes.goal: Evaluate agricultural transition pathways using coupled scenarios, lifecycle boundaries, uncertainty, and participatory criteria.
learning_outcomes: Construct conditional transition scenarios with transparent boundaries.
Analyze rebound, leakage, and distributional effects.
Critique lifecycle and system-level conclusions through sensitivity and participation.

lesson.overview: A sustainability transition changes practices, infrastructure, institutions, and incentives across a connected food system. Scenario analysis explores conditional futures rather than predicting one inevitable outcome. Lifecycle assessment defines a functional unit and boundaries, while consequential reasoning asks how a decision changes wider production, consumption, and land use. Rebound, leakage, distributional effects, and path dependence can alter an apparently favorable intervention. Graduate assessment makes assumptions inspectable, tests sensitivity and competing models, and includes affected stakeholders in defining outcomes instead of treating an optimization score as a complete public decision.
lesson.worked_example: A scenario reduces irrigation withdrawal per tonne through new equipment. If cheaper production expands the irrigated area, total withdrawals may fall less than expected or rise. A second scenario includes an area constraint. Comparing both reveals that technical efficiency and governance assumptions jointly determine the system outcome.
lesson.activity: Develop a transition brief comparing three fictional pathways for a region. Define the baseline, functional unit, land and water boundaries, adoption assumptions, social indicators, uncertainty ranges, and stakeholder perspectives. Perform a sensitivity analysis on one rebound mechanism and write a critique of the preferred pathway.
lesson.reflection: Which assumption makes your preferred future possible, and who has the power or resources to make it happen?

quiz.prompt: What is a scenario in this context?
choices: A conditional future under stated assumptions
A forecast with a guaranteed probability of one
A description independent of choices and conditions
quiz.answer: A conditional future under stated assumptions
quiz.explain: Scenarios explore what could follow if particular conditions and choices hold.

quiz.prompt: Efficiency lowers cost and encourages greater total resource use. What is this called?
choices: A boundary allocation
A sampling effect
A rebound effect
quiz.answer: A rebound effect
quiz.explain: Behavioral or economic responses can offset some or all expected resource savings.

quiz.prompt: Production moves outside the regulated region, shifting impacts there. What issue arises?
choices: Random error in the measurement instrument
Leakage across the policy boundary
Decoupling within the original process
quiz.answer: Leakage across the policy boundary
quiz.explain: A local reduction can be offset by displaced activity and impacts elsewhere.

quiz.prompt: Why distinguish attributional from consequential questions?
choices: Describing burdens differs from estimating decisions’ effects
Current burdens directly establish future causal responses
Both questions imply identical boundaries and counterfactuals
quiz.answer: Describing burdens differs from estimating decisions’ effects
quiz.explain: The questions imply different boundaries, counterfactuals, and treatment of system responses.

quiz.prompt: What does a sensitivity analysis reveal?
choices: Which stakeholders should receive decision authority
Whether the preferred pathway is ethically superior
How conclusions respond to changed assumptions
quiz.answer: How conclusions respond to changed assumptions
quiz.explain: Varying plausible assumptions shows dependence and possible fragility of conclusions.

quiz.prompt: Why include affected stakeholders in defining indicators?
choices: They replace the need to measure policy consequences
They reveal valued outcomes and overlooked burdens
They guarantee agreement over competing priorities
quiz.answer: They reveal valued outcomes and overlooked burdens
quiz.explain: Participation broadens the decision criteria and reveals perspectives without eliminating disagreement.

quiz.prompt: A transition locks farmers into expensive equipment and one supplier. Which concept is relevant?
choices: Path dependence
Sampling independence
Parameter identifiability
quiz.answer: Path dependence
quiz.explain: Past investments and institutional arrangements can constrain later choices.

quiz.prompt: A per-tonne impact falls but production doubles. What else must be calculated?
choices: The unchanged baseline intensity ranking
The production system’s average selling price
Total impact at the changed output scale
quiz.answer: Total impact at the changed output scale
quiz.explain: Total impact depends on both intensity and scale.

quiz.prompt: Why compare more than one plausible model?
choices: Model agreement proves the causal mechanism
Structural assumptions can change preferred pathways
Averaging models guarantees unbiased forecasts
quiz.answer: Structural assumptions can change preferred pathways
quiz.explain: Model-form uncertainty can be as important as parameter uncertainty.

quiz.prompt: Which recommendation best fits uncertain scenario evidence?
choices: A conditional choice with monitoring and revision triggers
A fixed promise that the preferred future will occur
A numerical ranking without explaining decision criteria
quiz.answer: A conditional choice with monitoring and revision triggers
quiz.explain: Transparent conditions and learning plans connect uncertain evidence to accountable decisions.

quiz.prompt: An irrigation technology reduces water withdrawal per tonne by 20%, while total output rises by 50%. Under proportional scaling, calculate the new withdrawal relative to baseline and explain the policy implication.
quiz.answer: Relative withdrawal is 0.8 times 1.5 = 1.2, or 120% of baseline. Total withdrawal rises by 20% despite the lower intensity, illustrating rebound or scale effects. The scenario needs system boundaries and governance assumptions rather than equating efficiency with absolute savings.
quiz.explain: Relative withdrawal is 0.8 times 1.5 = 1.2, or 120% of baseline. Total withdrawal rises by 20% despite the lower intensity, illustrating rebound or scale effects. The scenario needs system boundaries and governance assumptions rather than equating efficiency with absolute savings.

nodes.title: Environmental Research and Adaptive Management
nodes.goal: Design a reproducible research program that links causal evidence, monitoring, and revision of environmental decisions.
learning_outcomes: Distinguish ecological state from the observation process.
Design monitoring that tests competing hypotheses and informs decisions.
Critique causality, reproducibility, data governance, and transfer across scales.

lesson.overview: Environmental research often works with changing systems, limited replication, and decisions that cannot wait for perfect knowledge. Adaptive management is a structured learning process: state competing hypotheses, select actions and informative monitoring, evaluate outcomes, and revise decisions under explicit objectives. Merely changing a plan after disappointment is not sufficient. Research must separate detection from ecological state, account for dependence and missing data, and avoid interpreting every temporal change as an intervention effect. Graduate work publishes assumptions and negative results, protects sensitive ecological and community information, and states how findings might transfer across scales.
lesson.worked_example: A restoration project records more birds after habitat work, but observers also spend twice as long surveying. The increase in detections cannot be assigned entirely to ecological recovery. A revised protocol standardizes effort, estimates detection where feasible, uses comparison sites, and predefines what findings would trigger a change in management.
lesson.activity: Write a research proposal for a fictional restoration or agricultural intervention using synthetic data. Include competing hypotheses, comparison design, observation process, uncertainty analysis, reproducible workflow, data-governance plan, and a decision rule for adapting management. Peer-review your own strongest causal claim and revise it.
lesson.reflection: What observation would distinguish a change in the ecosystem from a change in your ability to detect it?

quiz.prompt: Survey effort doubles and species detections rise. What must be considered?
choices: Observation effort and ecological state
Ecological growth inferred directly from counts
Species abundance independent of survey methods
quiz.answer: Observation effort and ecological state
quiz.explain: Observation effort can change recorded detections without the same change in true abundance.

quiz.prompt: What makes management adaptive in a research sense?
choices: Periodic changes responding to the latest preference
A schedule for repeating the same reporting template
Hypotheses, monitoring, evaluation, and planned revision
quiz.answer: Hypotheses, monitoring, evaluation, and planned revision
quiz.explain: Adaptive management deliberately links action and learning to decision revision.

quiz.prompt: Why specify a decision trigger before examining outcomes?
choices: To eliminate the need to revise a hypothesis
To connect evidence and action transparently
To ensure that the intended outcome will occur
quiz.answer: To connect evidence and action transparently
quiz.explain: A predefined trigger reduces arbitrary reinterpretation while still allowing documented revision.

quiz.prompt: A before-after change occurs at one restored site. What is a causal limitation?
choices: Other time-varying causes could explain the change
Temporal ordering identifies the restoration effect
A single site supplies randomized treatment evidence
quiz.answer: Other time-varying causes could explain the change
quiz.explain: Without a credible counterfactual, background trends and co-occurring events remain plausible explanations.

quiz.prompt: Why consider detection probability in wildlife monitoring?
choices: Recorded counts directly equal ecological abundance
Detection probability is constant across survey effort
Observation differs from presence and abundance
quiz.answer: Observation differs from presence and abundance
quiz.explain: Imperfect detection can make observed counts differ from the underlying ecological state.

quiz.prompt: What should a reproducible analysis include?
choices: Summary tables, preferred hypotheses, and press releases
Data provenance, methods, code, and environment
Final figures, project title, and author affiliations
quiz.answer: Data provenance, methods, code, and environment
quiz.explain: Reproduction needs enough information to reconstruct transformations and results.

quiz.prompt: Why might exact locations of vulnerable species be restricted?
choices: Disclosure could expose vulnerable populations to harm
Coordinates are irrelevant to ecological replication
Scientific data become invalid when access is restricted
quiz.answer: Disclosure could expose vulnerable populations to harm
quiz.explain: Responsible data sharing balances reproducibility with concrete conservation and community concerns.

quiz.prompt: A null result has a wide uncertainty interval. What is an appropriate interpretation?
choices: The intervention has a precisely established zero effect
The missing significance proves a reversed effect
Important effects may remain compatible with the data
quiz.answer: Important effects may remain compatible with the data
quiz.explain: Imprecision can leave several substantively different effects compatible with the data.

quiz.prompt: Why report an unsuccessful intervention?
choices: It identifies the correct alternative mechanism alone
It supports learning and reduces selective evidence
It establishes that the intervention was misconduct
quiz.answer: It supports learning and reduces selective evidence
quiz.explain: Negative and mixed results help others understand limits and avoid publication bias.

quiz.prompt: A plot-scale result is applied across a whole watershed. What needs scrutiny?
choices: Scale-dependent processes and transfer assumptions
The display size and color of the watershed map
The alphabetical order of the sampling locations
quiz.answer: Scale-dependent processes and transfer assumptions
quiz.explain: Interactions, heterogeneity, and feedbacks can change when moving between scales.

quiz.prompt: Bird detections rise after restoration, but survey effort also doubles. Propose a study that separates ecological change from observation change and links findings to adaptive decisions.
quiz.answer: Standardize or model survey effort and detection probability, include suitable comparison sites, and quantify uncertainty about ecological state. Specify competing hypotheses and a monitoring protocol, then define decision triggers for revising management. The observation process must be distinguished from restoration impact.
quiz.explain: Standardize or model survey effort and detection probability, include suitable comparison sites, and quantify uncertainty about ecological state. Specify competing hypotheses and a monitoring protocol, then define decision triggers for revising management. The observation process must be distinguished from restoration impact.
